title: The human microbiome and chronic disease: ten strategic priorities for research and public health

summary: Camupepimut (ELI-002 7P) drives mutated KRAS (mKRAS)-specific T cell responses that correlated with disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS) in patients with mKRAS pancreatic adenocarcinoma (PDAC) in the phase 1 AMPLIFY-201 trial. In the phase 2 AMPLIFY-7P trial, patients with stage I-III KRAS-mutated PDAC without recurrence within 6 months of standard therapy were randomized 2:1 to camupepimut (n = 96) or standard-of-care/observation (n = 48). Stratification balanced nodal status. The primary DFS endpoint was not met (median 23.8 versus 21.2 months; HR 0.85, P = 0.5329). However, prespecified and exploratory analyses were informative. A numerical DFS advantage at 6 months of 14.0% (75.7% versus 61.7%; HR 0.55, P = 0.0557) corresponded to camupepimut dosing. Post hoc multivariate Cox regression analysis of DFS indicated an improved outcome for camupepimut (adjusted HR 0.47, P = 0.0086), a worse outcome for stage III disease (adjusted HR 2.29, P = 0.0127), an elevated baseline CA19-9 (adjusted HR 3.16, P < 0.0001) and baseline circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) positivity (adjusted HR 5.99, P < 0.0001). Prespecified subgroup analyses addressing prognostic and predictive factors suggested DFS benefit for camupepimut (ctDNA negative: HR 0.51, P = 0.0280; no prior radiation: HR 0.59, P = 0.0221). Exploratory analysis demonstrated that ex vivo mKRAS-specific T cell responses were robust (98.9%, 89/90) and associated with antigen spreading (86.7%, 13/15). In camupepimut-treated patients, mKRAS-specific T cell response >9.17-fold over baseline (82.2%, 74/90) correlated with improved DFS (HR 0.22, P < 0.0001), with the median DFS not reached versus 6.08 months for above and below 9.17-fold, respectively. Camupepimut safety was similar to observation, with grade ≥3 adverse events in 10.4% (10/96) versus 14.6% (7/48), and few serious AEs (6.3%, 6/96 versus 8.3%, 4/48; reflecting progression/surgical complication). These efficacy and immunogenicity signals will inform a refined strategy for a confirmatory phase 3 trial. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05726864 . As presented at the ESMO Congress 2026, in a randomized phase 2 trial evaluating an off-the-shelf lymph node-targeting peptide vaccine in patients with mutated KRAS pancreatic cancer within 6 months of standard curative intent therapy, the primary endpoint of disease-free survival was not met, but prespecified subgroup analyses showed significant disease-free survival benefit in the vaccine arm for patients with circulating tumor DNA-negative disease and in those without prior radiation treatment.
title: Lymph node-targeted, mKRAS-specific amphiphile vaccine in pancreatic cancer: the randomized phase 2 AMPLIFY-7P trial

summary: Invikafusp alfa (invika), a first-in-class, bispecific, dual T cell agonistic antibody selectively targeting Vβ6/Vβ10 T cell subsets, is being evaluated in START-001, a multicenter phase 1/2 monotherapy trial in participants with mostly immune checkpoint blockade (ICB)-resistant, antigen-rich solid tumors. Primary outcomes were safety/tolerability and recommended phase 2 dose (RP2D) in phase 1 and anti-tumor activity in phase 2. As of 12 March 2025, phase 1 completed dose escalation (n = 34) through dose levels of 0.01, 0.02, 0.04, 0.08, 0.12 and 0.16 mg kg−1 without reaching maximum tolerated dose, and initial phase 2 enrolled 18 participants. Two participants experienced reversible dose-limiting toxicities, one at each of the 0.08 mg kg−1 and 0.16 mg kg−1 dose levels. The most common treatment-related adverse event was cytokine release syndrome, mainly grades 1 and 2. No treatment-related deaths or non-laboratory grade 4 adverse events were reported. At the optimal biological doses (OBDs; 0.08 mg kg−1 and 0.12 mg kg−1) in combined phase 1 and phase 2 cohorts, the overall objective response rate was 14.8% (4/27), including confirmed partial responses in immunologically cold tumors, such as microsatellite stable colorectal cancer and programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)-negative non-small cell lung cancer. No objective responses were seen at doses lower than 0.08 mg kg−1. Invika selectively and potently expanded peripheral and intratumoral Vβ6/Vβ10 T cells, of a predominantly memory-like phenotype, dose-dependently, peaking at the OBDs. Pharmacodynamic increases in interferon-γ and soluble CD25 followed a similar pattern. Integrated analyses from safety, pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic and preliminary anti-tumor data supported the selection of 0.08 mg kg−1 as the RP2D. In conclusion, phase 1 of START-001 met its primary outcomes by demonstrating the acceptable safety profile of invika consistent with its mechanism of action and selecting an RP2D. Initial phase 2 results further corroborated the safety of invika and expanded its preliminary evidence of clinically meaningful anti-tumor activity in ICB-resistant solid tumors, supporting further evaluation in the ongoing phase 2. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05592626 . As presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology Congress 2026, in a phase 1/2 trial in participants with solid tumors, invika, a first-in-class bispecific agonistic antibody that selectively targets the prevalent Vβ6/Vβ10 T cell subsets, was well tolerated, enabling the selection of a recommended phase 2 dose for further testing, and showed a preliminary efficacy signal in both immunologically hot and cold tumors.
title: Bispecific dual T cell agonist invikafusp alfa in solid tumors: the phase 1/2 START-001 trial

summary: In patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) treated with chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy, factors associated with efficacy overlap with prognostic biomarkers. Currently, there is no consensus on optimal product characteristics. We analyzed the phenotypic attributes of the anti-CD19 CAR T therapy axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) from 580 patients with NHL across multiple clinical trials with long-term follow-up (median, 41.9 months). A high proportion of naive-like (CCR7+CD45RA+) T cells was the most significant feature associated with prolonged progression-free survival (PFS; hazard ratio = 0.46, 95% confidence interval: 0.31−0.68, P = 9.8 × 10−5, high versus low naive-like T cell groups) without impacting safety. The relationship between naive-like T cells and efficacy was independent of tumor microenvironment characteristics (assessed in 112 patients). In multivariate models, the naive-like phenotype outperformed clinicopathologic features such as inflammatory markers and tumor burden, remaining significant after adjusting for product expansion. An inverse correlation was observed between prior lines of therapy and the proportion of naive-like T cells in both product and matched apheresis samples, suggesting a benefit of earlier intervention. The key findings were validated in an independent cohort of 203 patients treated with axi-cel-based therapy or brexucabtagene autoleucel. Mass cytometry by time-of-flight analysis of products from a subgroup of 116 patients confirmed an association between a CD8 naive-like T cell phenotype lacking expression of exhaustion markers, such as TIGIT, LAG-3 and PD-1, and PFS. The evidence generated by this study has the potential to advance the development of more effective cellular therapies. A large comprehensive analysis of clinical trial samples from patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma who were treated with anti-CD19 CAR T therapy shows that a high proportion of naive-like and stem cell memory-like CCR7+CD45RA+ T cells in the pre-infusion CAR T product correlates with improved and prolonged clinical benefit, which was validated in an independent external cohort including different products.
title: Determinants of response to CAR T cell therapy in a multicenter, multi-trial cohort analysis of patients with lymphoma
